extracted.intended_audience: parties and counsel in patent litigation (Northern District of California)
extracted.subtask_short: stipulated protective order for patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: A template Stipulated Protective Order governing designation, handling, disclosure, challenge, storage, filing, and final disposition of confidential, highly confidential (AEO), and source-code material in patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Protected Material under seal
rubrics_metrics.description: A Party may not file in the public record any Protected Material without written permission from the Designating Party or a court order; requests to file under seal must comply with Civil Local Rule 79-5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protected Material may only be filed under seal pursuant to a court order authorizing sealing of the specific Protected Material at issue. A sealing order will issue only upon a request establishing that the Protected Material is privileged, protectable as a trade secret, or otherwise entitled to protection under the law. If a Receiving Party’s request to file Protected Material under seal pursuant to Civil Local Rule 79-5(e) is denied, the Receiving Party may file the Protected Material in the public record pursuant to Civil Local Rule 79-5(e)(2) unless otherwise instructed by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final disposition and return/destruction of Protected Material
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 60 days after final disposition each Receiving Party must return all Protected Material to the Producing Party or destroy such material and submit a written certification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘All Protected Material’ includes copies, abstracts, compilations, summaries and any other format reproducing or capturing Protected Material. The written certification must (1) identify (by category, where appropriate) all the Protected Material that was returned or destroyed and (2) affirm the Receiving Party has not retained any copies, abstracts, compilations, summaries or other reproductions. Counsel are entitled to retain archival copies of pleadings, motion papers, transcripts, legal memoranda, correspondence, deposition and trial exhibits, expert reports, attorney work product, and consultant/expert work product even if such materials contain Protected Material; archival copies remain subject to the Protective Order as set forth in Section 4 (DURATION).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Protected Material and confidentiality levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Protected Material means Disclosure or Discovery Material designated as “CONFIDENTIAL” or “HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS’ EYES ONLY” (and optionally “HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – SOURCE CODE”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘CONFIDENTIAL’ covers information qualifying for protection under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(c). ‘HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS’ EYES ONLY’ is extremely sensitive Confidential Information disclosure of which to another Party would create a substantial risk of serious harm that could not be avoided by less restrictive means. Optional source code category is for confidential proprietary source code and associated materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the Order's protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Protections cover Protected Material and (1) any information copied or extracted from Protected Material; (2) all copies, excerpts, summaries, or compilations; and (3) any testimony, conversations, or presentations that might reveal Protected Material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protections do not cover information (a) in the public domain at time of disclosure or becoming public through lawful means, or (b) known to the Receiving Party prior to disclosure or obtained lawfully from a source under no confidentiality obligation. Any use of Protected Material at trial shall be governed by a separate agreement or order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of confidentiality obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidentiality obligations remain in effect even after final disposition until the Designating Party agrees otherwise in writing or a court order directs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final disposition is the later of (1) dismissal of all claims and defenses (with or without prejudice) and (2) final judgment after exhaustion of appeals, rehearings, remands, trials, or reviews, including time limits for filing motions or extensions. Archival copies retained by counsel remain subject to this Protective Order as set forth in Section 4 (DURATION).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise of restraint in making designations
rubrics_metrics.description: A Designating Party must take care to limit designations to specific material that qualifies for protection and avoid sweeping non-qualifying material into the Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass, indiscriminate, or routinized designations are prohibited. Designations shown to be clearly unjustified or made for an improper purpose (e.g., to encumber or retard case development or impose unnecessary expenses) can expose the Designating Party to sanctions. If a Designating Party learns a designation was mistaken, it must promptly notify other parties and withdraw the designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner and timing of documentary designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure or Discovery Material that qualifies for protection must be clearly designated before disclosure or production by affixing the legend “CONFIDENTIAL” or “HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS’ EYES ONLY” to each page containing protected material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a portion of a page qualifies, the Producing Party must clearly identify the protected portion(s) (e.g., markings in the margins) and specify the level of protection for each portion. Documents made available for inspection need not be designated until after the inspecting Party identifies what it wants copied and produced; during inspection the material is deemed “HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS’ EYES ONLY.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation procedures for depositions and transcripts
rubrics_metrics.description: For testimony, the Designating Party must identify on the record before the close of the deposition/hearing/other proceeding all protected testimony and specify the level of protection; or, if impractical, invoke a right to identify within 21 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantial portions may qualify, the Designating Party may have up to 21 days to identify protected portions; only portions designated within 21 days are covered. Alternatively, a Designating Party may specify the entire transcript be treated as CONFIDENTIAL or HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – AEO. Parties must give notice if a proceeding will include Protected Material so only authorized individuals who signed Exhibit A are present. Transcripts containing Protected Material must have an obvious legend on the title page and a following list of all pages/line numbers designated; transcripts prepared before expiration of a 21-day period are treated as fully HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – AEO until designation period expires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of non-documentary tangible items
rubrics_metrics.description: For information produced in non-documentary form and other tangible items, the Producing Party must affix in a prominent place on the exterior of the container the legend “CONFIDENTIAL” or “HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS’ EYES ONLY.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a portion of the information or item warrants protection, the Producing Party should identify the protected portion(s) and specify the level of protection to the extent practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadvertent failures to designate
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely-corrected inadvertent failure to designate qualified information does not, by itself, waive the Designating Party’s right to protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon timely correction of a designation, the Receiving Party must make reasonable efforts to ensure the material is treated in accordance with the Order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for challenging confidentiality designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any Party or Non-Party may challenge a designation at any time; prompt challenge is required when necessary to avoid substantial unfairness, unnecessary burdens, or significant disruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party does not waive its right to challenge by electing not to mount a prompt challenge unless promptness is necessary to avoid prejudice or burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-and-confer requirement for challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Challenging Party must initiate dispute resolution by written notice describing each designation challenged and the basis, and must confer directly (voice to voice) within 14 days of service of notice to attempt to resolve the challenge in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written notice must recite that the challenge is made in accordance with this paragraph. The Challenging Party must explain its basis and give the Designating Party opportunity to reconsider; a Challenging Party may proceed only after engaging in the meet-and-confer or demonstrating the Designating Party is unwilling to participate in a timely manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial intervention and deadlines for retaining confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: If parties cannot resolve a challenge, the Designating Party must file and serve a motion to retain confidentiality under Civil Local Rule 7 (and comply with Civil Local Rule 79-5, if applicable) within 21 days of the initial notice of challenge or within 14 days of agreement that meet-and-confer will not resolve the dispute, whichever is earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each motion must be accompanied by a competent declaration affirming meet-and-confer compliance. Failure to file within the deadlines automatically waives the confidentiality designation for each challenged designation. The burden of persuasion is on the Designating Party. Frivolous challenges or those for improper purpose may expose the Challenging Party to sanctions. Until the court rules, parties must continue to afford the material the level of protection asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted uses and secure storage of Protected Material
rubrics_metrics.description: Protected Material may be used only for prosecuting, defending, or attempting to settle this litigation and must be stored and maintained in a secure manner limiting access to authorized persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When litigation has terminated, Receiving Parties must comply with final disposition provisions. It may be appropriate under certain circumstances to require electronic Protected Material to be stored in password-protected form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted disclosure categories for CONFIDENTIAL material
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless ordered otherwise or permitted in writing by the Designating Party, CONFIDENTIAL material may be disclosed only to specified categories of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorized recipients include: (a) Receiving Party’s Outside Counsel of Record and necessary employees who signed Exhibit A; (b) officers, directors, employees (including House Counsel) for whom disclosure is reasonably necessary and who signed Exhibit A; (c) Experts who signed Exhibit A and need disclosure; (d) the court and its personnel; (e) court reporters, professional jury/trial consultants, and Professional Vendors who signed Exhibit A; (f) deposition witnesses during their depositions who signed Exhibit A (pages of testimony revealing Protected Material must be separately bound and not further disclosed); and (g) the author or recipient of a document or a custodian who otherwise possessed the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted disclosure categories for HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS’ EYES ONLY
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless ordered otherwise or permitted in writing by the Designating Party, AEO material may be disclosed only to a narrower set of recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorized recipients include: (a) Receiving Party’s Outside Counsel of Record and necessary employees who signed Exhibit A; (b) optionally, Designated House Counsel who meet specified conditions (no involvement in competitive decision-making, need-to-know, signed Exhibit A, and compliance with approval procedures); (c) Experts who signed Exhibit A and for whom approval procedures in paragraph 7.4 have been followed; (d) the court and its personnel; (e) court reporters, their staff, professional jury/trial consultants, and Professional Vendors who signed Exhibit A; and (f) the author or recipient or custodian who otherwise possessed the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for approving disclosure of AEO to Designated House Counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: To disclose AEO material to Designated House Counsel, the requesting Party must make a written request to the Designating Party with the full name, city/state of residence, and detailed description of current and reasonably foreseeable future primary job duties to determine involvement in competitive decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Designating Party has 14 days to object in writing detailing grounds. If objected to, the parties must meet and confer (voice-to-voice) within seven days; if unresolved, the requesting Party may file a motion describing the circumstances, reasons disclosure is reasonably necessary, risk assessment, and additional means to reduce risk, accompanied by a competent declaration describing meet-and-confer efforts. The party opposing disclosure bears the burden of proving the risk of harm outweighs the need for disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for approving disclosure of AEO to Experts
rubrics_metrics.description: To disclose AEO material to an Expert, the requesting Party must make a written request identifying categories of AEO information sought to be disclosed, the Expert’s full name and residence, current resume, current employer(s), compensation or funding received in the Expert’s areas of expertise during preceding five years, and litigation in which the Expert offered testimony during the preceding five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Designating Party has 14 days to object in writing. If objected, parties must meet and confer within seven days; if unresolved, the requesting Party may file a motion under Civil Local Rule 7 seeking permission to disclose, with the motion describing necessity, risk assessment and alternatives and accompanied by a declaration of meet-and-confer efforts. If the Expert believes some information is subject to third-party confidentiality, the Expert should disclose what can be provided and parties should meet and confer regarding the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution bar for recipients of AEO
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent written consent from the Producing Party, any individual who receives access to AEO (or optionally AEO/source code) information shall not be involved in prosecution of patents or patent applications relating to the subject matter of the highly confidential technical information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Prosecution’ includes directly or indirectly drafting, amending, advising, or otherwise affecting the scope or maintenance of patent claims (original prosecution, reissue, reexamination, etc.). Prosecution does not include representing a party challenging a patent before an agency. The Prosecution Bar begins when access is first received and ends two (2) years after final termination of the action. It may be appropriate to require an 'Ethical Wall' for counsel who receive AEO information. Parties may also limit access of Designated House Counsel to AEO/source code under certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source code designation and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: If production of source code becomes necessary, a Producing Party may designate source code as “HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – SOURCE CODE.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source code designated as such shall be subject to all protections afforded to HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – ATTORNEYS’ EYES ONLY (including the optional Prosecution Bar) and may be disclosed only to individuals to whom AEO information may be disclosed, as set forth in Paragraphs 7.3 and 7.4, with the exception that Designated House Counsel shall not have access to HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL – SOURCE CODE. Parties may also consider tailored procedures for source code (not detailed in this excerpt).
